question: A bungee cord is not really a rope. Its core is a thick bundle of hundreds of thin strands of which stretchy material?
source_excerpt: one or more rubber strands inside a woven cotton or polypropylene cover

extra.why_interesting: People picture a bungee cord as a strong rope. It is really a giant bundle of the same stretchy stuff as a rubber band, and that is why the jump ends in a bounce, not a snap.
extra.verification_notes: Bungee cord cores are bundles of rubber (latex) strands inside a braided sheath; no contradicting or newer information found (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bungee_cord).

explanation: The cord is basically a huge bundle of rubber bands, so it can stretch to several times its resting length. That stretch spreads the stop over many metres, which is why it feels like a bounce instead of a jolt.

question: Bungee jumping copies an old ritual on a Pacific island in Vanuatu, where men dive head-first from tall wooden towers. What is tied to their ankles instead of an elastic cord?
source_excerpt: performed by the men of the southern part of Pentecost Island... jumpers with vines tied to their ankles

extra.why_interesting: Bungee seems like a modern thrill sport that depends on hi-tech elastic. Its ancestor is a centuries-old island ritual that uses nothing but plants, and the player can work out the answer by asking what stretchy thing grows in a jungle.
extra.verification_notes: Pentecost Island naghol land divers jump from wooden towers with vines tied to their ankles, per Wikipedia's land diving article (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Land_diving).

explanation: The divers use fresh forest vines, which have just enough give to stop them right above the ground. Visitors who saw the ritual helped inspire the first rubber-cord jumps.
